To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

protein interfaces are slightly more conserved in both sequence alignments of close homolog/orthologs (P = 0.0003) and diverse homologs (P < 0.0001) than the rest of a protein surface, and that the interface is not significantly more conserved (P > 0.05) than other surface patches.

the protein–protein interface is slightly more conservative in sequence than the remainder of the surface when using either a close homolog/ortholog alignment or a diverse homolog/paralog alignment; however, when a protein–protein interface patch is among the most conservative surface patches, it is rarely significantly more conservative than other surface patches; and the most conservative surface patch tends to be part or all of an enzyme active center.

(a) protein interfaces are slightly more conserved in both sequence types, (b) interfaces are not significantly more conserved on average than other patches of surface, (c) interfaces are not more conserved than random surface patches, (d) the most conserved patches of surface tend to overlap with enzyme active sites, and (e) the obligate interface has more conserved buried residues than transient interfaces.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether protein–protein interfaces are distinguishable from other surface patches in a protein by their degree of sequence conservation.
the conservation of protein–protein interfaces and how this relates to the conservation of the surface of the protein as a whole.
the conservation of protein interfaces, which are the sites of interaction of proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
interfaces are more conserved in some alignments than in others, and that conservation is not sufficient to accurately predict interfaces.
protein–protein interfaces are not significantly more conserved in either sequence or structural alignments.
interfaces are not significantly more conserved in protein sequences than the rest of a protein surface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protein interfaces are more conserved in both sequence and structure than the rest of protein surface.
protein interfaces are not more conserved than surface patches, but that the most conserved patches do tend to be interfaces.

while protein interfaces are generally more conserved than their surrounding surface, this is not a universal rule and that other factors, such as the presence of a binding partner, are required to make this distinction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interface is not always the most conserved region of the protein surface and that the use of conservation scores for interface prediction is not a panacea.

protein interfaces are not more conserved than surface patches, and thus residue conservation alone is insufficient to predict protein–protein interfaces.
